clue.text: Spine-chiller produced with professional collaborator?

definitions.meaning: a tale of the supernatural meant to frighten the reader
a narrative written with the help of a hired writer who goes uncredited, a so-called ghostwriter

explanation.surface: A thriller written with a paid partner.
explanation.definitionFit: A tale of spectres is the classic spine-chiller, and a book ghostwritten is one produced with a hidden professional collaborator.

clue.text: "All hygienes have their " (Vladimir Nabokov)

parts.note: a quotation from Nabokov with its last word left blank: the solver supplies the missing word, a scavenging animal

explanation.surface: A quotation from Nabokov with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a fill-in-the-blank quotation; the missing word echoes the sound of 'hygienes', which is the joke of the line.
explanation.definitionFit: The blank in Nabokov's line is filled by the laughing scavengers of the African plains, punning on the sound of the preceding word.

clue.text: Vita Sackville-West's sirens from South America

definitions.text: Vita Sackville-West's sirens from South America

parts.words: Vita Sackville-West's sirens from South America
parts.note: points to the title of Sackville-West's 1924 novella set in Ecuador, whose first word means tempters or sirens

explanation.surface: Enchantresses from Latin America in a work by Vita Sackville-West.
explanation.walkthrough: Vita Sackville-West wrote the novella Seducers in Ecuador; Ecuador is the 'South America' of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Sirens are tempters who lure men astray, the figures named in the first word of Sackville-West's Ecuador title.

clue.text: Carl a stoic? Not quite (more in the manner of Xenophon's master)

definitions.text: in the manner of Xenophon's master

indicators.note: a stoic that is not quite right is out of order, so these letters are to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Carl is nearly a Stoic, more like the teacher of Xenophon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not quite' suggests trimming a letter, but nothing is removed: it signals an anagram of CARL A STOIC. Xenophon was a pupil of Socrates.
explanation.definitionFit: Xenophon studied under Socrates, so behaving in that philosopher's questioning manner is the adjective formed from his name.

clue.text: Close kin of Electra in forest, escaping censure

indicators.note: the word in tells us the answer sits inside the run of letters of forest and escaping

explanation.surface: A relative of Electra hides in a wood to avoid blame.
explanation.walkthrough: The brother of Electra in Greek myth was tried for matricide and acquitted, so 'escaping censure' fits him too.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Electra's brother avenged their father Agamemnon with her help, so he is her close kin.

clue.text: Abraham Cahan's protagonist begins year early (knowing little)

indicators.note: begins here means we take the opening letter of each of the following four words

explanation.surface: A hero who starts the year ahead, though he knows little.
explanation.walkthrough: Abraham Cahan's 1896 novel is Yekl: A Tale of the New York Ghetto; the initials of 'year early knowing little' spell the hero's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of Cahan's first novel is a Jewish immigrant in New York, the protagonist the clue names.

clue.text: Irish dramatist who made the discovery in 1763, they say

definitions.text: Irish dramatist who made the discovery in 1763, they say

parts.words: Irish dramatist who made the discovery in 1763, they say
parts.note: plays on Boswell's Life of Johnson, where in 1763 Johnson spoke of the Irish actor and elocutionist Thomas, father of the playwright, as naturally dull

explanation.surface: An Irish playwright who reportedly found something out in 1763.
explanation.walkthrough: The surname is shared by Richard Brinsley, the dramatist, and his father Thomas, whom Johnson discussed in Boswell's 1763 entries.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Brinsley, author of The Rivals and The School for Scandal, was a Dublin-born playwright bearing this surname.

clue.text: The part-timer estimated by Thomas Shadwell

parts.note: a temp is a temporary worker, a part-timer
EST is the usual abbreviation for estimated

explanation.surface: A temporary worker is assessed by the Restoration poet Thomas Shadwell.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Shadwell produced the 1674 operatic adaptation of Shakespeare's late romance of the shipwreck on Prospero's island.
explanation.definitionFit: Shadwell's best-known stage work is his operatic adaptation of Shakespeare's island play, so a work by him.

clue.text: Wilder day

parts.note: points to the title of Thornton Wilder's 1967 novel, which names a day by its number in the sequence

explanation.walkthrough: Wilder looks like a comparative adjective, but it is Thornton Wilder, whose novel is The Eighth Day.
explanation.definitionFit: Thornton Wilder's novel is titled after the day following the seventh, so the ordinal is the word that pairs with 'day'.

clue.text: "I'm very brave generally …only today I happen to have a " (Lewis Carroll)

definitions.text: "I'm very brave generally …only today I happen to have a " (Lewis Carroll)

parts.words: "I'm very brave generally …only today I happen to have a " (Lewis Carroll)
parts.note: a line spoken by Tweedledum in Through the Looking-Glass with its last word left blank: his excuse for avoiding the battle

explanation.surface: A quotation from Lewis Carroll with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: Tweedledum offers this pain in the head as his excuse for not fighting his brother.
explanation.definitionFit: Tweedledum's excuse is a pain in the head, the common complaint that fills the blank in Carroll's line.

clue.text: Let loser change into armoured footwear

indicators.note: change tells us to alter the order of the letters of let loser

explanation.surface: A defeated knight is allowed to swap into his metal boots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change into' reads as changing clothes; 'change' signals the anagram of LET LOSER and 'into' links it to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plate-armour shoe covering the foot, worn by medieval knights.

clue.text: Enquire, say, for graceful pilgrim?

indicators.note: say signals that the word for enquire is to be heard as spoken, not spelled

parts.note: to enquire is to ask

explanation.surface: A question about what to call an elegant pilgrim.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Aske led the Pilgrimage of Grace, the 1536 northern rising against Henry VIII, so he was a pilgrim of 'Grace'.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Aske was the leader of the Pilgrimage of Grace, so the clue's 'graceful pilgrim' is a pun on that rising.

clue.text: Epithets unfortunately eject divas

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things going wrong, so the letters of eject divas are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Insults are hurled when divas are sadly thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfortunately' signals the anagram of EJECT DIVAS.
explanation.definitionFit: An epithet is a descriptive word or phrase attached to a name, a describing word in grammar terms.

clue.text: He arranges strange duel on motorway by river (despite 10)

definitions.text: He arranges strange duel on motorway by river (despite 10)

parts.note: the Tweed is a river on the border between England and Scotland

indicators.note: strange signals that the letters of duel come out in an unusual order

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for motorway, as in M1

explanation.surface: A man sets up an odd fight on a highway near a river, though he has a sore head.
explanation.walkthrough: The river Tweed comes first, then LEDU (the anagram of DUEL, from 'strange') on M. Tweedledum agreed to fight his brother in spite of his headache, the answer to 10.
explanation.definitionFit: In Through the Looking-Glass the Carroll twin who agrees to battle his brother over a rattle, while pleading a sore head.

clue.text: "In deep of night when / Hath locked up mortal sense " (Milton)

definitions.text: "In deep of night when / Hath locked up mortal sense " (Milton)

parts.words: "In deep of night when / Hath locked up mortal sense " (Milton)
parts.note: lines from Milton's masque Arcades with a word left blank: the state that dulls the senses at night

explanation.surface: Lines from Milton with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: The lines come from Arcades, spoken by the Genius of the Wood; the missing word is the sleepiness that shuts down the senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Milton's blank is the heaviness of sleepiness that locks up the senses at night.

clue.text: Miss Mitford as usurer's daughter

definitions.meaning: the Mitford sister who wrote The American Way of Death
the moneylender Shylock's daughter in The Merchant of Venice, who elopes with Lorenzo

explanation.surface: One of the Mitford sisters cast as the moneylender's girl.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the Mitford sisters, a writer and activist, shares her first name with Shylock's daughter in The Merchant of Venice.

clue.text: He felt that discretion was not the better part of biography

definitions.text: He felt that discretion was not the better part of biography

parts.words: He felt that discretion was not the better part of biography
parts.note: echoes the preface to Eminent Victorians, where Lytton wrote that discretion is not the better part of biography

explanation.surface: A biographer who preferred candour to tact.
explanation.walkthrough: The line twists the proverb 'discretion is the better part of valour'; Lytton's preface to Eminent Victorians made it a manifesto for frank biography.
explanation.definitionFit: Lytton, the Bloomsbury biographer of Eminent Victorians, made this remark the creed of irreverent life-writing.

clue.text: Sort of mini ode Scott introduced for Abel Sampson

indicators.note: sort means put in order, so the letters of mini ode are to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A short poem of a kind that Walter Scott wrote for a character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of' signals the anagram of MINI ODE. Abel Sampson is the tutor in Scott's Guy Mannering, always called by this Scots word for a schoolmaster.
explanation.definitionFit: Scott gave the Scots word for a schoolmaster to Abel Sampson, the tutor in Guy Mannering, as his usual title.

clue.text: Keats told Fanny Brawne that he had left no such work behind him

definitions.text: Keats told Fanny Brawne that he had left no such work behind him

parts.words: Keats told Fanny Brawne that he had left no such work behind him
parts.note: refers to Keats's 1820 letter to Fanny Brawne lamenting that he had written nothing that would last forever

explanation.surface: Keats wrote to his love that he had left no lasting work.
explanation.walkthrough: Keats wrote: 'I have left no immortal work behind me', ironic given his later fame.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats feared he had written nothing undying, the adjective for work that lives forever.

clue.text: First illuminated in early ms

definitions.meaning: the large decorated capital letter that opens a page of a medieval manuscript

explanation.surface: The opening letter of an old manuscript was decorated.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means coming at the start, and also names the ornamented first letter in medieval manuscripts.

clue.text: Whence Shakespeare drew his leading character, in general

definitions.text: Whence Shakespeare drew his leading character, in general

parts.words: Whence Shakespeare drew his leading character, in general
parts.note: a Roman general named for his capture of the Volscian town of Corioli, the title figure of a Shakespeare tragedy

explanation.surface: Where Shakespeare got his main character from.
explanation.walkthrough: The hero takes his name from Corioli, the town he captured; he is a general, which the clue's 'in general' hints.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Roman tragedy takes its title from the general Caius Marcius, named for the town of Corioli he stormed.

clue.text: Dana served before it

parts.note: refers to Richard Henry Dana's memoir of life as a common sailor, Two Years Before the ...

explanation.surface: A sailor did his service in front of something.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Henry Dana's 1840 memoir is Two Years Before the Mast, about life as an ordinary seaman, who lodged forward of the ship's spar.
explanation.definitionFit: Ordinary seamen were quartered forward of the ship's tall spar, so Dana served before it.

clue.text: Consult an eminent Arabist to reveal an audience for Grand Vizier's daughter

indicators.note: to reveal shows that the answer lies exposed within the letters of consult an

explanation.surface: Ask a learned Arabist about who listened to the vizier's daughter.
explanation.walkthrough: Scheherazade, the Grand Vizier's daughter in The Arabian Nights, told her tales nightly to the ruler.
explanation.definitionFit: Scheherazade, the vizier's daughter in The Arabian Nights, told her stories to the ruler, so he was her audience.

clue.text: Fleur Adcock's sort of book

parts.note: points to the title of Fleur Adcock's 1986 poetry collection, The ... Book

explanation.surface: A type of volume by the poet Fleur Adcock.
explanation.walkthrough: Fleur Adcock's collection is The Incident Book; an incident book is also one where events are logged.
explanation.definitionFit: Fleur Adcock's poetry collection takes its title from the log in which events at a school or workplace are recorded.

clue.text: Sufficient for Shakespeare

parts.note: an Elizabethan word meaning enough, as used in Shakespeare's plays

explanation.surface: Enough for the Bard.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic form meaning enough, common in Shakespeare's time.

clue.text: It was on the cards for Dennis

definitions.text: It was on the cards for Dennis

parts.words: It was on the cards for Dennis
parts.note: points to Nigel Dennis's 1955 satirical novel Cards of ...

explanation.surface: Something was bound to happen to Dennis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the cards' means likely, but here it is literal: Nigel Dennis wrote the novel Cards of Identity.
explanation.definitionFit: Nigel Dennis's novel Cards of Identity puts this word, meaning who one is, on its cards.

clue.text: Violinist appearing in Graham Greene's Comedians

indicators.note: appearing in shows that the answer turns up among the letters of Greene's Comedians

explanation.surface: A violinist plays a part in Graham Greene's novel The Comedians.
explanation.walkthrough: Georges Enesco was a Romanian violinist and composer.
explanation.definitionFit: George Enescu, often spelt Enesco, was a celebrated Romanian violinist and composer.

clue.text: Predator thus advanced by Powys

parts.note: a wolf is a predator
so means thus
to advance money is to lend it, so advanced gives lent

explanation.surface: A hunting animal pushed forward in this way by the writer Powys.
explanation.walkthrough: John Cowper Powys's 1929 novel is Wolf Solent.
explanation.definitionFit: Wolf Solent is the 1929 novel of John Cowper Powys, so a work by him.
